normalized.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; put the cash into the software business, which can break even without new funding
executive_summary: The market grows about 40% a year, but no operator has yet shown it can make money in it – Zipcart loses $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 on each order (p. 5–8)
At benchmark inputs an order loses about $6.2 after site costs; the plan needs every driver above the best site – Break-even would need a $63 basket, against the $34 median (p. 10–17)
Few customers keep ordering, so the $38 it costs to win each one is slow or impossible to recover – Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three (p. 19–22)
The launch leaves about 6 months of runway even if all goes to plan; the software can break even on current cash – The software breaks even in early 2029 with about $5.4M left (p. 24–29)
Decline the launch; put $0.8M a year into the software and store-based delivery for grocers, with gates to reopen – Reopen only when a customer site makes money after site costs (p. 31–34)

slides.title: Parcelbird Now: should we launch quick-commerce grocery delivery in 2027?
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027, using only its $12.0M of cash and keeping 12 months of runway?
evidence: Decision maker: Board of Parcelbird (two founders, two investors), deciding whether to fund the launch

Success criteria: A path to profitability within the current $12.0M of cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; Orders that make money after site costs on inputs already observed, not only in the plan
Timing: Board meeting, January 2027
Out of scope: A new funding round; Other cities; Non-grocery delivery

Sub-questions: 1 Is the market growing, and has any operator shown it can make money in it? 2 Can an order make money after paying for the rider and the dark store? 3 Do customers order often enough to repay what it costs to win them? 4 Does the plan keep 12 months of runway, and is it the best use of the cash? 5 What should the board decide in January 2027, and what would reopen the question?

slides.title: The market
The market is growing fast, but no operator has yet shown it can make money in it

claims.claim: Sales are growing about 40% a year, as the founders say, and nearly tripled in three years
evidence: 41.7% growth in US quick-commerce grocery sales in 2025

claims.claim: Both incumbents lose money on every order, and the regional one is retreating from its cities
evidence: 36.4% of QuickBasket's cities were closed in 2025

claims.claim: Growth shows customers want the service; it does not show that anyone can run it at a profit
Not tested: the founders' view that no operator owns the Midwest; the pack holds no competitor data for the three cities

claims.claim: US sales nearly tripled between 2022 and 2025
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $ billions: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1

2024: the slowest year, and still up 38%

slides.title: 1b: Both incumbents lose money on every order, and their EBITDA losses equal a quarter to nearly half of revenue

evidence: EBITDA, % of revenue, 2025: Zipcart -25.83%; QuickBasket -45.71%

claims.claim: Being 5.7 times larger has not made Zipcart profitable, and QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: 1b: Zipcart's one profitable city shows the price of profit: a new fee and fewer promotions cost it 14% of orders

claims.claim: The national leader lost money on every order
evidence: Lost $1.90 on each order across the business in 2025
EBITDA loss of $310M on $1.2B of revenue
The densest city was the one best placed to turn positive

claims.claim: It charged more and discounted less
evidence: Added a new $3.99 service fee to every order
Cut promotions to 1% of order value
Made both changes in its densest city only

claims.claim: Impact
evidence: $0.4 contribution per order in that city, Q4 2025
−14% change in that city's orders after the changes

claims.claim: The profit came from charging more and serving fewer orders, not from scale

slides.title: The market
Only the founders' untested plan makes an order profitable after paying for the rider and the dark store

evidence: −$6.2 contribution per order after site costs, benchmark medians

evidence: $2.02 contribution per order after site costs, founders' plan

slides.title: 2a: At benchmark medians, every order loses about $6.2 once the rider and the dark store are paid for

claims.claim: At benchmark medians, every order loses about $6.2 once the rider and the dark store are paid for

evidence: $63.4 basket needed to break even at benchmark costs, against the $34 median
Rider: 43% of the cost to serve an order, set by pay per hour and drops per hour
Dark store: a fixed cost, so only more orders a day spread it thinner
Break-even: would need a basket 1.9 times the median, beyond the best site's $42

slides.title: 2a: Orders pay their own way only with a $42 basket and 3 deliveries per rider-hour, a pairing no site has achieved

claims.claim: Pop-up test basket loses money at every productivity level
Benchmark median basket loses money even at the best rider productivity
Best observed basket turns positive only at 3.0 an hour; the best basket and the best rider productivity came from different sites
Founders' plan positive from 3.0 an hour, a level only the best site reached
Figures are before dark-store costs
evidence: Other inputs at the benchmark: 27% goods margin, $1.99 net delivery fee, $3.10 picking, $1.30 payment and packaging, $17.75 rider cost an hour
Before the $1.15M yearly dark-store cost, which adds $3.5 an order at 900 orders a day

slides.title: 2b: The founders' plan needs every driver above the best site observed, all at the same time

claims.claim: The founders' plan is above the best on all four, at once
evidence: Benchmark median: $34, 6%, 2.4, 900
Pop-up test: $31, 12%, 2.1, 280 — Below the median on all four
Best observed: $42, 6%, 3, 1,400 — Best basket and best density came from different sites
Founders' plan: $45, 2%, 3.5, 1,800
Benchmark ranges across the 14 sites: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour and 400–1,400 orders per site a day; the plan's 1,800 a day is 1.3 times the top of the range

slides.title: 2b: Rider productivity and basket size carry over half of the plan's swing from loss to profit

claims.claim: Rider productivity and basket size carry over half of the plan's swing from loss to profit
evidence: Gain per order vs benchmark median, $: Rider productivity 2.3244; Basket size 2.31; Promotions 1.8; Density 1.7504
56.6% of the plan's per-order swing comes from riders and basket
Steps applied in the order basket, promotions, riders, density; changing the order moves value only between basket and promotions

claims.claim: Four assumptions of similar size, none of them observed
evidence: Rider productivity: 3.5 drops an hour, above the top of the 1.9–3.0 range at any site
Basket size: $45, above the best site's $42 and the pop-up's $31
Promotions and density: 2% promotions are a sixth of the pop-up's spend, and 1,800 orders a day is twice the median

slides.title: 2b: Missing either the basket or the rider target on its own wipes out the plan's profit per order

claims.claim: Missing either the basket or the rider target on its own wipes out the plan's profit per order
evidence: Plan contribution after site costs with one input at median, $: Basket at $34 -0.7318; Riders at 2.4 an hour -0.3062; Promotions at 6% 0.2182; Density at 900 a day 0.2678; Plan as presented 2.0182

claims.claim: The plan's margin of safety is a single assumption
evidence: Basket: at the $34 median the order loses money even with promotions at 2%
Riders: 2.4 an hour is the median of 14 sites, and the pop-up managed 2.1
Promotions or density: either one missed alone leaves under $0.3 of profit an order

claims.claim: Treat month-18 profit as a best case that needs every target met together

slides.title: 2c: Parcelbird's own pop-up ran below the benchmark on every driver and lost about $12.6 an order

claims.claim: Parcelbird's own pop-up ran below the benchmark on every driver
evidence: Columbus pop-up test, one temporary site, six weeks, autumn 2026
280 orders a day — 31% of the 900 benchmark median; below the 400 low end of the benchmark range; a six-week test, still ramping up
2.1 orders per rider-hour — against 2.4 at the median site; each order carried $8.5 of rider cost
12% of order value spent on promotions — twice the 6% benchmark, six times the plan; first-order credits drove early volume; the plan assumes 2%

claims.claim: Lost about $12.6 an order after site costs (team estimate)
evidence: −$6.2 contribution before site costs, with benchmark margin, picking and rider pay + −$6.4 site cost per order: $0.65M a year over 280 orders a day = −$12.6
Twice the loss at the median site
A $31 basket, against $34 at the median
The pack gives no pop-up figure for goods margin, delivery fee, picking, rider pay or payment cost; benchmark values used

slides.title: 2d: Copying Zipcart's fee and promotion cut would still leave each order about $1.05 short after site costs

claims.claim: Copying Zipcart's fee and promotion cut would still leave each order about $1.05 short after site costs
evidence: −$2.7 contribution before site costs, benchmark median + $5.7 from Zipcart's moves ($3.99 fee and promotions cut from 6% to 1% of a $34 basket) − $4.1 dark-store cost per order once orders fall 14% = −$1.05

claims.claim: The estimate is generous to the launch
evidence: The $3.99 fee is kept in full, with no payment cost on it
Orders fall 14% as in Zipcart's city, so the $1.15M site cost is spread over 774 orders a day

claims.claim: Pricing can close most of the gap, but the lost orders raise the store cost per order and keep it negative

slides.title: The market
Few Columbus customers keep ordering, which leaves the $38 cost of winning each one unrecovered

claims.claim: Interest is real, but repeat use is far below what the survey suggests

slides.title: 3a: Survey enthusiasm overstates real use: only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering by month three

claims.claim: Survey enthusiasm overstates real use
evidence: 44% of surveyed residents aged 25–39 say they would order at least weekly (1,500 respondents); a survey of the target age group, not of customers; says nothing about price or fees

3.1 orders a month by those who stay — below the survey's 'at least weekly'; top-up use, not the weekly shop
0.7 orders a month per customer acquired, from month three (22% staying × 3.1 orders)
The survey and the pop-up measure different groups

slides.title: 3a: Pop-up orders grew quickly, yet even the final week ran at under half a median site's daily volume

claims.claim: Growth was real but started from a low base
evidence: Orders a day by week (team estimate): 178.6; 210.7; 248.6; 293.4; 346.2; 408.5
45.4% of the 900-a-day median, in the final week

slides.title: 3b: Even on the founders' economics, a new customer takes about 15 months to repay the $38 it cost to win

claims.claim: Even on the founders' economics, a new customer takes about 15 months to repay the $38 it cost to win
evidence: $38 ÷ 0.7 orders a month ÷ $3.8 contribution per order before site costs (plan) = 14.8 months

claims.claim: At the benchmark the cost is never repaid
evidence: At the benchmark median each order loses $2.7 before site costs, so every order deepens the loss
After site costs the plan earns $2.0 an order and the wait stretches to about 28 months
Orders in months one and two are left out; retention after month three is held flat

slides.title: The market
The software business, not the launch, offers a path to profit that keeps the runway rule

Scaling the software is the only option that passes both of the investors' tests
